config.title: Multiple State Variables

intro.title: Multiple State Variables
intro.body: In this lesson, you'll build an interactive user profile form that manages multiple pieces of information simultaneously, such as a user's name, email, and age. You'll learn how to use multiple useState hooks in a single React component to track different state variables independently. This approach allows each piece of data to be updated separately while maintaining the component's overall state. You'll practice creating separate state variables, updating them with individual setter functions, and displaying the current values in your JSX. By the end of this lesson, you'll understand how to organize and manage complex component state using multiple useState declarations instead of cramming everything into a single state object.
intro.usecase: Multiple state variables are essential in complex React applications where different UI elements need independent state management. In e-commerce sites, you might track separate state for shopping cart items, user authentication status, search filters, and modal visibility all within the same component. Social media dashboards often manage multiple states simultaneously - like post data, user preferences, notification counts, and loading states for different sections. Forms frequently require tracking individual field values, validation errors, and submission status as separate state variables to provide responsive user feedback.

objectives: Initialize multiple independent state variables within a single React component
Implement separate event handlers to update different state values
Construct user interface elements that display multiple state variables simultaneously
Apply state updates that modify one state variable without affecting others
Configure controlled input elements that bind to different state variables
Manipulate component behavior by coordinating updates across multiple state values
Integrate multiple useState hooks to manage complex component data

steps.title: Import React and useState
steps.hint: Use the import statement to bring in React and the useState hook from the 'react' library.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: importing multiple items
import { Component, Fragment } from 'react';
steps.expectedOutcome: React and useState are imported and ready to use for building components with state.
successCriteria: React and useState are imported from 'react'.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure you're importing both React and useState from the 'react' library.
steps.feedbackWrong: import both React and useState from 'react' using the import statement.

steps.title: Create the main App component
steps.instruction: Create a functional component named App that returns JSX
steps.hint: Define a function named App that returns some JSX content. You can start with a simple div element.
steps.expectedOutcome: A functional component named App is created that returns JSX
successCriteria: App component is defined and returns JSX content
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure your App component returns some JSX content.
steps.feedbackWrong: create a function named App that returns JSX. You can use either function declaration or arrow function syntax.

steps.title: Initialize the first state variable for count
steps.instruction: Inside the App component, use useState to create a count state variable initialized to 0
steps.hint: Use the useState hook with 0 as the initial value. Remember to destructure both the state variable and its setter function.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: creating a state variable for age
const [age, setAge] = useState(25);
steps.expectedOutcome: A count state variable is created using useState, initialized to 0, with both the state variable and setter function properly destructured
successCriteria: useState is called with 0 as initial value and destructured into count and setCount variables
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure you're destructuring both the state variable (count) and the setter function (setCount) from useState(0).
steps.feedbackWrong: use useState with 0 as the initial value and destructure it into [count, setCount]. This creates both the state variable and the function to update it.

steps.title: Initialize the second state variable for name
steps.instruction: Add a second useState call to initialize a name state variable with an empty string
steps.hint: Use useState again with an empty string as the initial value. Destructure it into name and setName variables.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: creating another state variable
const [color, setColor] = useState('blue');
steps.expectedOutcome: A second state variable named 'name' is initialized with an empty string using useState
successCriteria: The name state variable is created using useState with an empty string as initial value
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure you're using useState to create the name variable with an empty string as the initial value.
steps.feedbackWrong: use useState to create the name state variable. Initialize it with an empty string: useState('')

steps.title: Define the increment handler function
steps.instruction: Create a function named incrementCount that increases the count value by 1 using setCount
steps.hint: Define a function that calls setCount with count + 1 to increment the current count value
steps.expectedOutcome: A function named incrementCount is defined inside the App component that calls setCount to increase count by 1
successCriteria: Function incrementCount is created and calls setCount with count + 1
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure your function calls setCount with count + 1 to increment the value.
steps.feedbackWrong: The increment handler should be a function that calls setCount(count + 1) to increase the count by 1.

steps.title: Define the name change handler function
steps.instruction: Create a function named handleNameChange that takes an event parameter and updates the name state with the event target value
steps.hint: Use setName to update the name state. Access the input value with event.target.value
steps.expectedOutcome: A function that can handle input changes and update the name state variable
successCriteria: handleNameChange function is defined and updates name state with event.target.value
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure your function takes an event parameter and calls setName with event.target.value.
steps.feedbackWrong: create a function that takes an event parameter and uses setName to update the state with the input value.

steps.title: Create the component structure with div container
steps.instruction: Update the return statement to include a div container that wraps the existing h1 heading
steps.hint: Replace the current div and h1 with a new div that contains the h1 heading as its child element
steps.expectedOutcome: The component returns JSX with a div container that wraps the h1 heading
successCriteria: The return statement contains a div element that wraps the h1 heading with the text 'Multiple State Variables'
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure your div container properly wraps the h1 heading element.
steps.feedbackWrong: The component should return a div element that contains the h1 heading as its child. Check that your JSX structure has the div as the parent element.

steps.title: Display the count state value
steps.instruction: Add a paragraph element inside the div that displays the current count value
steps.hint:
Use JSX to create a

element and include the count variable inside curly braces to display its value
steps.expectedOutcome: The count state value is displayed in a paragraph element within the component
successCriteria: A paragraph element is added that displays the current count value using JSX curly braces
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure you're displaying the count variable inside JSX curly braces within a paragraph element.
steps.feedbackWrong:
add a paragraph element that displays the count variable. Use

{count}

to show the current count value.

steps.title: Add increment button and wire onClick handler
steps.instruction: Add a button element with the text 'Increment Count' that calls the handleIncrement function when clicked.
steps.hint: Use the <button> element with an onClick attribute to wire up the event handler.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: button with click handler
<button onClick={handleSubmit}>Submit Form</button>
steps.expectedOutcome: A button labeled 'Increment Count' is added that will call the handleIncrement function when clicked.
successCriteria: Button element with text 'Increment Count' and onClick handler connected to handleIncrement function
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure your button has the correct text and is connected to the handleIncrement function with onClick.
steps.feedbackWrong: The button needs to have 'Increment Count' as the text and onClick={handleIncrement} to connect it to the handler function.

steps.title: Add name input field and wire onChange handler
steps.instruction: Add an input field below the increment button that displays the current name value and calls handleNameChange when the user types in it.
steps.hint: Create an input element with type='text', value set to the name state, and onChange set to handleNameChange.
steps.analogousExample:
// Similar: input field with value and onChange
<input type="text" value={userInput} onChange={handleInputChange} />
steps.expectedOutcome: The app will have an input field that shows the current name value and updates the name state when the user types in it.
successCriteria: An input element is added with type='text', value={name}, and onChange={handleNameChange}.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Nice! Proceed to the next step.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start! Make sure your input has the value attribute set to {name} and onChange set to {handleNameChange}.
steps.feedbackWrong: The input needs to be connected to the name state. Set value={name} and onChange={handleNameChange} to make it a controlled component.
